title: Norisring 2013: Ekström first across the line, race left without a winner
dek: Mattias Ekström crossed the line first at the Norisring but was excluded for a parc fermé breach; pole-sitter Robert Wickens finished as the best-placed classified driver and the race went unwon.

chapters.title: Half-way point on the streets of Nuremberg
text: The fifth of the ten DTM races of 2013 took place on Sunday 14 July on the Norisring, the 2.3-kilometre street circuit in Nuremberg that marks the half-way stage of the season. Mike Rockenfeller and Bruno Spengler arrived level on 59 points at the head of the championship, with Gary Paffett third on 47 after his Lausitzring win four weeks earlier and Christian Vietoris fourth on 40.

The track has its own character: two long straights, tight corners, concrete walls and qualifying gaps measured in thousandths of a second. It had also been Mercedes territory, with the three-pointed star taking the lion's share of the wins over the previous decade, while Audi had waited since 2002 for a win at what is effectively its home round. Jamie Green, known as the King of the Norisring, was on the Audi side for the first time in 2013.

The race distance was 83 laps, with two mandatory tyre changes and the Drag Reduction System available to help with overtaking. The weekend drew 126,000 spectators and temperatures climbed above 30 degrees on Sunday.

chapters.title: Wickens takes a first pole as Rockenfeller is shut out
text: Saturday's qualifying produced the first pole position of Robert Wickens's DTM career. The Canadian had been in the top six in every segment and then set 48.384 in the single-lap final shoot-out, which left his fellow Canadian Spengler 0.059 seconds behind in the Schnitzer BMW and gave a Canadian front row. Paffett took third for HWA, 0.076 off the pole, and Edoardo Mortara was the best Audi in fourth, 0.106 down.

Behind them, Pascal Wehrlein started fifth, Andy Priaulx sixth for the RMG BMW team after setting the quickest time in the second segment, and Daniel Juncadella seventh, the highest grid slot of his DTM career. Filipe Albuquerque, Mattias Ekström, who had spun at the last corner of the second segment, and Vietoris completed the top ten.

The big names to suffer were Audi's. Rockenfeller was knocked out in the first segment after 19th fastest, saying the set-up was never right, and slipped to 21st on the grid, while Miguel Molina lined up last. Green, the circuit's specialist, failed to reach the third segment and started 14th. Five of the six Mercedes cars were in the top ten, and Wickens said he was lost for words when Paffett told him the pole was his.

chapters.title: Two early safety cars rewrite the strategy
text: Timo Scheider never completed a lap, and the opening phase was dominated by two early safety car periods that blew the strategy open. Ekström gained four places on the first lap, moving from ninth to fifth, and went on to pass both Spengler and Wickens. Mortara switched to the faster option tyres on lap 5, and after the neutralisations he was leading the field from lap 14.

Rockenfeller's recovery was the sharpest tactical move. Starting from the back, he took both of his mandatory stops in direct succession on laps 13 and 15 while the field was slow, and was suddenly in the hunt for points. Wickens, who had lost places, said he dropped as low as 14th at one stage.

The second safety car was caused by Martin Tomczyk, who retired after contact with Green. BMW's Jens Marquardt said afterwards that the two interventions opened up strategy options, but that the team chose not to gamble on one set of tyres lasting, and several rivals who did so passed its cars over the afternoon.

chapters.title: Ekström and Mortara pull clear
text: Once the track went green, Ekström and Mortara used the option tyres to build a gap to the cars behind. Ekström ran an unusually long stint, taking the lead on lap 64 when he passed Mortara, who was struggling with his brakes, and holding it through his second stop, which came on lap 78. Rockenfeller and Paffett, who had completed both stops under the second safety car, were his main rivals, but he built enough margin for the final stop.

Mercedes' HWA squad had its own plan. Vietoris, who started tenth, was sent back out on options after his stop and made up ground as others struggled with brakes and tyres, and he set the fastest lap of the race on lap 9. Green, meanwhile, covered only 65 of the 83 laps, with a gear-shift problem.

chapters.title: Mortara and Paffett collide twice
text: With Ekström clear, the fight for second turned violent. Mortara, who had left the pits right behind Paffett after the stop, ran into the back of the Mercedes going into the Grundig corner on lap 79. The contact let Vietoris and Wickens through, and when Paffett fought back to third the two collided again coming out of the Bahnhof corner on lap 82. Both were left two laps down, classified 17th and 18th, with Mortara's podium chance gone.

Ekström crossed the line 2.646 seconds clear of Wickens on the road, with Vietoris a further 3.636 seconds behind the Canadian. Juncadella took fourth for Mücke, and Rockenfeller, who had started 21st, finished fifth to take sole command of the championship from the back row. Spengler was sixth, the best BMW, followed by Roberto Merhi and Joey Hand.

chapters.title: A victory removed, and a race without a winner
text: The celebrations did not last. Before the podium ceremony the stewards had opened an inquiry into whether Ekström had broken the parc fermé rules after water was poured into the pockets of his race suit before the weighing. More than five hours after the finish the stewards excluded him, leaving Wickens to be named the provisional winner, and Ekström was also fined 1,000 euros for failing to put his steering wheel back properly. Audi announced an appeal almost at once. Wickens, promoted that night, said he was thrilled to have won even after the wait, and that HWA had changed his strategy cleverly after the second safety car.

The DMSB appeal court ruled on 30 July. It upheld the exclusion, but decided that Ekström had gained no competitive advantage and had won on the track under fair conditions, so no other driver was moved up. The Norisring race therefore had no official winner, and Wickens is classified second as the best-placed driver. Audi said it would accept the decision.

The standings were not affected at the top. Rockenfeller led with 69 points, Spengler had 67, Vietoris 55, Paffett 47 and Wickens 45, with Farfus on 33. Spengler said he had expected much more at a track he liked, and described eight points as better than none. Mercedes motorsport chief Toto Wolff called it a great spectacle but regretted that Paffett had left without points and said he would review the footage of the collision with Mortara. Audi's Dieter Gass called the contacts at the end a pity, because they cost the brand a second car on the podium.
The next race was at Moscow Raceway on 4 August. Mercedes left Nuremberg with four cars in the top seven, including Wickens, Vietoris, Juncadella and Merhi, even though Paffett had scored nothing.

facts.v: The DMSB appeal court upheld Ekström's exclusion on 30 July 2013 but moved nobody up, so Wickens is the best-placed classified driver.
